articles.title: Emanuel Cacho: propostas para rodovias e transporte em Sergipe | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato do PSDB participou da série com os candidatos ao governo de Sergipe; calendário de entrevistas vai até sábado (19) com a exibição de uma entrevista gravada.
articles.summary: O candidato Emanuel Cacho (PSDB) detalhou propostas para as eleições em Sergipe, focando na duplicação de rodovias como a BR-235 e na melhoria do transporte público.
articles.body:
Emanuel Cacho ( PSDB ), candidato ao governo de Sergipe, falou nesta sexta-feira (18), em entrevista ao SE2, da TV Sergipe, sobre a desistência da candidatura de Suely Barreto e afirmou que pretende duplicar rodovias e organizar transporte metropolitano.

O SE2 iniciou na última segunda-feira uma série de entrevistas ao vivo com os candidatos ao governo. Cada candidato tem 10 minutos para apresentar propostas e responder a perguntas sobre os principais temas do estado. As entrevistas são conduzidas pelo jornalista Lyderwan Santos.

19/09: Taty Cristina de Jesus (Democracia Cristã)

Candidato ao governo de SE Emanuel Cacho (PSDB) concede entrevista ao jornalista Lyderwan Santos, no SE2. — Foto: Mira Marques/g1 SE

Possibilidade de desistência e lançamento de candidatura

Questionado se pareceria inconsistente para o eleitor o candidato, a poucos dias da convenção partidária, ter dado declarações públicas sobre a possibilidade de desistência do projeto próprio para apoiar a candidatura de outro partido e nos momentos finais lançar a sua para o governo, ele explicou que exatamente para não sinalizar uma possível falta de convicção é que formalizou a candidatura.

“[...] a divulgação dessa desistência, que não foi desistência, realmente me incomodou muito porque houve uma precipitação. A notícia tem que ser dada na hora certa depois de discutida”, disse.

Ele citou ainda que nunca desistiu de seus projetos, mas antes de anunciar a candidatura era necessário afinar o rumo do projeto junto ao seu grupo político.

Durante a entrevista, o candidato foi questionado sobre a saída da vice-governadora Suely Barreto, que renunciou ao cargo alegando publicamente que não tinha espaço para opinar nem participar das decisões.

“Parece que os problemas eles ficaram parecidos, nós tivemos uma eleição da prefeita de Aracaju e o vice-prefeito queria sentar para dividir a cadeira com ela. Então nós tínhamos um tempo de 30 segundos apenas para divulgar a nossa candidatura e aí houve um certo incômodo [...] coisa natural que é da política [...] ela foi a única candidata a vice que apareceu no programa eleitoral sozinha. Foi divulgado exatamente no dia que ela renunciou”.

Ele citou ainda que, após a saída de Suely, o vereador Fabrício Menezes entrou para a disputa do cargo.

Ainda durante a entrevista, Emanuel foi questionado sobre como ele planeja diminuir a desigualdade apontada por ele no “momento de recuperação econômica”, no plano de governo.

“Eu falo que Sergipe teve algumas oportunidades. Nós tivemos um governante da qualidade de João Alves, que trouxe todas as coisas boas que tem em Sergipe foram trazidas por ele. Nós temos hoje oportunidades de negócio de repente, do dia pra noite, você está vendo as coisas melhorarem [...] quando eu fui secretário de Justiça, eu consegui um aumento pros policiais militares que trabalhavam pra mim de 150% [...] então é isso, eu gosto de melhorar a vida das pessoas”, disse.

Emanuel Cacho disputa o governo de Sergipe pelo PSDB — Foto: Mira Marques/g1

Sobre a proposta prevista no plano de governo dele para elaborar um programa de duplicação das principais rodovias estaduais, Emanuel foi perguntado sobre quais trechos serão priorizados.

“Em primeiro lugar eu não consigo compreender como alguém governou Sergipe e não viu que a nossa cidade com maior volume de negócios, que é Itabaiana, a BR-235, ela não é duplicada [...] A BR-101, Lagarto, subindo ali pra Simão Dias, e a gente vai fazer uma coisa que os Estados Unidos fez na década de 30, 40 que foram as grandes rodovias que elevaram os Estados Unidos a esse desenvolvimento que eles têm”, afirmou.

Ainda sobre transporte, o candidato foi questionado sobre como ele pretende reorganizar o sistema metropolitano do transporte coletivo na prática.

“Eu sempre vi a coisa mais óbvia de Sergipe. Nós temos uma rede ferroviária que foi desativada criminosamente que levava até o centro da cidade, que ia até as duas fronteiras de Sergipe. Simplesmente desativaram e o estado não assumiu esse ônus [...] nós precisamos trazer o transporte público de qualidade para fluir do interior pra capital, todos com ar-condicionado [...] Essa é uma proposta que eu falei no primeiro dia do governo, fazer o investimento imediato no transporte público do interior pra capital”, explicou.

Nas considerações finais, Emanuel Cacho afirmou que essa é uma eleição que é do mesmo grupo polarizado, que “se dividiram agora, mas eles estavam juntos sempre” e que ele é uma opção viável. O candidato reforçou ainda que sua candidatura está mantida e aprovada de forma legal.

articles.title: CIW 2026 encerra edição histórica com mais de 23 mil participantes | G1
articles.standfirst: Terceira edição reuniu mais de 200 empresas e startups, 250 palestrantes e 130 horas de conteúdo; evento consolida Campinas como polo de inovação e tecnologia
articles.summary: Terceira edição reuniu mais de 200 empresas e startups, 250 palestrantes e 130 horas de conteúdo; evento consolida Campinas como polo de inovação e tecnologia
articles.body:
CIW 2026 encerra com sucesso de público e presença de autoridades — Foto: Crédito: ppcfilms

O Campinas Innovation Week (CIW) 2026 encerrou nesta sexta-feira (18) sua terceira edição com números que demonstram a dimensão alcançada no calendário de inovação, tecnologia e negócios de Campinas e região.

Ao longo da semana, o evento reuniu mais de 23 mil pessoas no Pátio Ferroviário, no Prédio do Relógio, para acompanhar uma programação que contou com mais de 200 empresas e startups, mais de 250 palestrantes e 130 horas de conteúdo, além de experiências, networking, demonstrações tecnológicas e oportunidades de negócios.

Realizado pela Prefeitura de Campinas, por meio da Secretaria Municipal de Desenvolvimento Econômico, Tecnologia e Inovação, e executado pela Associação Comercial e Industrial de Campinas (ACIC), o tema deste ano foi “O Amanhã é Nosso”, oferecendo discussões sobre o fomento de toda a cadeia da tecnologia e inovação, com impacto nos negócios de Campinas e região.

Palestra do Google na parte da tarde focou na IA para Empreender — Foto: Crédito: ppcfilms

“O CIW ampliou o espaço de Campinas como ponto de encontro entre empresas, startups, universidades, centros de pesquisa, investidores, empreendedores, poder público e sociedade, com uma programação gratuita e extremamente relevante sobre os caminhos para o desenvolvimento econômico e tecnológico da região e do Brasil”, destaca Adriana Flosi, secretária de Desenvolvimento Econômico, Tecnologia e Inovação de Campinas e vice-presidente da ACIC.

Influencer David Brazil animou o público com seu estilo único — Foto: Crédito: ppcfilms

A programação foi organizada em cinco trilhas: Ecossistema, Ciência e Políticas Públicas; Negócios, Investimento e Varejo; Impacto, Pessoas e Experiência; Conectividade; e Conexões Globais. Entre os assuntos abordados estiveram inteligência artificial, startups, investimentos, transformação digital, sustentabilidade, agricultura digital, internacionalização, cidades inteligentes, blockchain, economia circular, criatividade e futuro do trabalho.

“O Campinas Innovation Week mostra, na prática, a força que existe quando empresas, startups, universidades, investidores e poder público se encontram em um mesmo ambiente. Chegamos ao encerramento desta terceira edição com um evento maior, mais diverso e conectado às necessidades de quem empreende e transforma a economia”, destaca a presidente da ACIC, Nina Bertelli.

Para ela, um dos diferenciais desta edição foi mostrar que inovação não se resume às novas tecnologias.

“O CIW aproximou ciência, negócios, cultura, empreendedorismo, sustentabilidade e desenvolvimento social, com experiências imersivas e demonstrações de tecnologias que certamente serão levadas como experiências pelo público presente. Para a ACIC, participar dessa construção é reafirmar nossa vocação de contribuir para que Campinas e toda a região avancem juntas”

Autoridades marcaram presença no encerramento do CIW 2026 — Foto: Crédito ppcfilms

A programação também abriu espaço para o protagonismo feminino, com o Elas Conectam, e para iniciativas de impacto social e econômico. A Economia Solidária, por exemplo, participou com 13 empreendedores que comercializaram produtos de artesanato e alimentação durante os cinco dias do evento.

Outro destaque foi a presença de povos originários, com culinária, artesanato e uma reflexão sobre a relação entre ancestralidade, conhecimento e tecnologia.

CIW 2026 contou com 23 mil pessoas durante os quatro dias de ação que contou com muitas palestras e networking — Foto: Crédito: ppcfilms

O CIW também serviu como espaço para ampliar a articulação regional. Durante o evento, prefeitos da Região Metropolitana de Campinas aprovaram a criação do RMC Deep Tech Valley, proposta de hub metropolitano voltado ao desenvolvimento e à instalação de empresas de tecnologia na região. A iniciativa prevê ações conjuntas, incluindo estímulo a leis municipais de inovação e ao uso de sandbox regulatório.

A agenda de Conexões Globais também colocou em pauta internacionalização, cooperação e atração de investimentos, aproximando o ecossistema campineiro de oportunidades além das fronteiras nacionais.

Para a ACIC, a realização do evento reforça a aproximação entre o ambiente tradicional de negócios e a nova economia. Um dos exemplos foi a Rodada de Negócios da ACIC, realizada nesta sexta-feira, que reuniu empresários, empreendedores, executivos, investidores e startups em encontros voltados à geração de oportunidades comerciais.

“Encerramos esta edição mostrando que Campinas tem um ecossistema capaz de reunir conhecimento, tecnologia, empreendedorismo, investimento e desenvolvimento econômico em um mesmo espaço. Mais de 23 mil pessoas participaram dessa construção, e o resultado é uma cidade ainda mais conectada e preparada para discutir os desafios e as oportunidades do futuro”, destaca Adriana Flosi.

Acadêmicos do Tucuruvi alegrou o público no encerramento do CIW 2026 — Foto: Crédito: ppcfilms

Depois de uma semana dedicada ao conhecimento, às conexões e aos negócios, o CIW 2026 encerrou a programação com uma apresentação da escola de samba Acadêmicos do Tucuruvi, em uma participação especial que reforça a proposta de integrar diferentes manifestações e experiências ao ambiente de inovação. O dia teve ainda a presença do influencer David Brazil, convidado especial, e do prefeito de Campinas, Dário Saadi.

articles.title: Entenda investigação sobre mortes de elefantas em santuário de MT | G1
articles.standfirst: Ibama investiga desde dezembro de 2025 as mortes das elefantas Pupy e Kenya. Licença do Santuário de Elefantes chegou a ser suspensa, mas foi restabelecida após autoridades sanitárias descartarem risco à saúde dos animais.
articles.summary: Ibama investiga desde dezembro de 2025 as mortes das elefantas Pupy e Kenya. Licença do Santuário de Elefantes chegou a ser suspensa, mas foi restabelecida.
articles.body:
A chegada do elefante Sandro , de 54 anos, ao Santuário de Elefantes Brasil, em Chapada dos Guimarães , a 65 km de Cuiabá, nesta sexta-feira (18), voltou a atenção para as investigações envolvendo o local, iniciadas após as mortes de duas elefantas africanas no fim de 2025 .

O Instituto Brasileiro do Meio Ambiente e dos Recursos Naturais Renováveis (Ibama) informou ao g1 nesta sexta-feira que a investigação sobre as mortes de Pupy, de 35 anos , e Kenya, de 44 anos , ainda está em andamento.

A apuração começou em dezembro de 2025 . Na ocasião, o Ibama realizou uma fiscalização no santuário e informou ter encontrado estruturas consideradas adequadas, além de profissionais habilitados, como biólogos e veterinários.

Segundo o instituto, muitos dos animais recebidos pelo santuário são idosos, passaram anos em circos ou outros tipos de cativeiro e possuem histórico de saúde delicado . Por isso, as condições anteriores de cada elefante também precisam ser consideradas na investigação das mortes .

Pupy morreu após colapsar repentinamente e Kenya morreu quatro dias depois de ser diagnosticada com problemas respiratórios e dores nas articulações.

A investigação levou a Secretaria de Estado de Meio Ambiente de Mato Grosso (Sema-MT) a suspender, de forma cautelar, a autorização para que o santuário recebesse novos animais .

A licença, no entanto, foi restabelecida em fevereiro deste ano , depois que autoridades sanitárias de Mato Grosso concluíram que não havia risco à saúde dos elefantes e permitiram novamente a chegada de animais ao local.

De acordo com o Ibama, a atualização mais recente do caso é de janeiro deste ano, quando o santuário apresentou documentos ao instituto sobre os protocolos de manejo, assistência veterinária e medidas sanitárias adotados no local . A documentação detalhou, entre outras medidas, procedimentos de quarentena e desinfecção.

Segundo o Ibama, as análises ambientais apresentadas não detectaram um grupo de bactérias chamado Mycobacterium do complexo tuberculosis nas amostras avaliadas. O resultado, porém, ainda não permite concluir o que provocou as mortes de Kenya e Pupy.

Isso porque, de acordo com o instituto, os laudos de necropsia das duas elefantas ainda não estavam concluídos na documentação analisada. Dessa forma, não foi possível estabelecer uma conclusão definitiva sobre as causas das mortes nem determinar eventual relação entre os óbitos e as condições de manejo do santuário.

Antes e durante a suspensão temporária da autorização para receber novos elefantes, o santuário foi alvo de questionamentos sobre o funcionamento do local.

Na época, o Santuário de Elefantes Brasil rebateu as acusações feitas contra o local nas redes sociais . A organização afirmou que as alegações não tinham fundamento e disse ser alvo de uma campanha de descrédito que buscava impedir a chegada de novos animais.

O santuário também criticou a suspensão determinada pela Sema-MT e afirmou que a medida não afetava os elefantes que já viviam no local.

"Infelizmente, as entidades oficiais responsáveis acabaram cedendo a essa retórica. Amplificada pela pressão pública e pelas limitações do período de festas, uma decisão apressada da Sema, órgão estadual regulador do Brasil, resultou na suspensão temporária de nossa licença, afetando nossa capacidade de receber novos elefantes. Essa decisão não impacta em nada os elefantes que já vivem no santuário", afirmou.

Em fevereiro, com o restabelecimento da licença, a organização afirmou que a decisão reforçava a capacidade técnica e a transparência das práticas adotadas e destacou que os procedimentos seguiam protocolos exigidos pelas autoridades responsáveis.

Elefante Sandro após a chegada em seu recinto em Chapada dos Guimarães (MT) — Foto: Victoria Oliveira/g1

Sandro deixou Sorocaba (SP) na quarta-feira (16) com destino a Mato Grosso, após uma determinação do Tribunal de Justiça de São Paulo (TJ-SP). O elefante vivia no Zoológico Municipal Quinzinho de Barros desde os anos 1980, e a transferência para o santuário encerrou uma longa disputa judicial relacionada ao bem-estar do animal.

A carreta com a caixa de transporte deixou o zoológico por volta das 12h10. Um grupo contrário à transferência protestou durante a saída, e a Polícia Militar usou spray de pimenta para dispersar os manifestantes.

Depois de cerca de cerca de três dias de viagem, Sandro chegou nesta sexta-feira ao Santuário de Elefantes Brasil , em Chapada dos Guimarães.

A saída da caixa ocorreu de forma espontânea, sem que o animal fosse forçado pelas equipes responsáveis pelo acompanhamento, assim que o recinto foi aberto, às 13h31, o elefante saiu em menos de um minuto, surpreendendo a todos.

Santuário de Elefantes Brasil (SEB), em Chapada dos Guimarães (MT) — Foto: Reprodução

O Santuário de Elefantes Brasil (SEB) é o primeiro santuário destinado a elefantes da América Latina . O projeto é conduzido pelo Global Sanctuary for Elephants (GSE) e pela ElephantVoices, organizações internacionais voltadas à conservação e ao bem-estar desses animais.

A organização não tem fins lucrativos e recebe elefantes que viveram em cativeiro , oferecendo espaço e acompanhamento para a recuperação física e comportamental dos animais. Diferentemente de um zoológico, o santuário não é aberto à visitação pública . Os elefantes circulam pelas áreas disponíveis e podem permanecer afastados dos tratadores e escondidos na vegetação.

A proposta é justamente evitar que os animais continuem sendo tratados como atração depois de anos vivendo em circos, zoológicos ou outros ambientes de cativeiro.

O público pode acompanhar parte da rotina dos elefantes pelas redes sociais e pelo site do projeto, onde são publicados relatos e vídeos feitos durante os cuidados com os animais. O santuário também mantém uma campanha de adoção simbólica, por meio da qual interessados podem contribuir financeiramente com os cuidados dos elefantes que vivem no local.

articles.title: Dinamarca e Groenlândia dizem que acordo com EUA reforça segurança | G1
articles.standfirst: Governos dizem que pacto será assinado na próxima semana durante Assembleia Geral da ONU. Texto ainda será analisado pelo Parlamento antes de entrar em vigor.
articles.summary: Governos dizem que pacto será assinado na próxima semana durante Assembleia Geral da ONU. Texto ainda será analisado pelo Parlamento antes de entrar em vigor.
articles.body:
Dinamarca e Groenlândia elogiaram nesta sexta-feira (18) o acordo de segurança fechado com os Estados Unidos que envolve a ilha. O governo dinamarquês afirmou que o tratado reconhece a soberania do território, ao mesmo tempo que amplia a segurança na região.

Mais cedo, o presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump , disse que o acordo dará aos americanos controle sobre a segurança e outras necessidades relacionadas à defesa da Groenlândia "para sempre".

A Groenlândia é uma ilha que faz parte do Reino da Dinamarca, mas tem governo autônomo.

Os EUA já demonstraram interesse em controlar ou adquirir o território no passado, principalmente por razões de segurança.

O assunto voltou a ganhar força no ano passado, quando Trump começou a defender a anexação da Groenlândia pelos EUA.

Atualmente, os norte-americanos mantêm uma base militar na região.

O governo da Dinamarca não deu detalhes sobre o texto do acordo, mas afirmou que o documento deve ser assinado na próxima semana, durante a Assembleia Geral da ONU. Segundo a primeira-ministra do país, Mette Frederiksen, o tratado vai fortalecer a segurança no Ártico e no Atlântico Norte.

"É um acordo que fortalece nossa segurança comum no Ártico e na região do Atlântico Norte e, portanto, também é bom para a Otan e para a Europa", afirmou.

"O acordo ao mesmo tempo reconhece a soberania e a integridade territorial do Reino e o direito do povo groenlandês à autodeterminação."

O primeiro-ministro da Groenlândia, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, disse que o acordo com os EUA respeita e reconhece os interesses da Groenlândia. Segundo ele, a iniciativa será benéfica a "todos".

Segundo Trump, o acordo fechado determina que nenhum adversário dos EUA poderá manter uma base ou presença militar na Groenlândia, nem fazer investimentos considerados sensíveis no território, sem autorização do governo americano.

"Começaremos imediatamente o processo de desenvolvimento de uma grande presença militar na parte apropriada da Groenlândia, que possui muitas dessas áreas", afirmou.

Ainda na publicação, Trump disse que o acordo representa um "sonho realizado" para os Estados Unidos e classificou o anúncio como "histórico" e "especial". Segundo ele, o acordo é "infinito" e não tem prazo para acabar.

Depois da assinatura, o texto ainda terá de passar pelos procedimentos parlamentares necessários para entrar em vigor.

Vista de Nuuk, capital da Groenlândia, em 9 de fevereiro de 2025 — Foto: Sarah Meyssonnier/Reuters

A Groenlândia está geograficamente localizada no continente norte-americano, mas mantém fortes vínculos com a Dinamarca. A ilha, que foi uma colônia dinamarquesa, passou a integrar o Reino da Dinamarca em 1953 e segue a Constituição dinamarquesa.

Em 2009, a Dinamarca autorizou a Groenlândia a formar um governo próprio e autônomo, abrindo a possibilidade de uma declaração de independência por meio de referendo.

Enquanto isso, os Estados Unidos consideram a Groenlândia um território estratégico para a própria segurança nacional. A ilha poderia abrigar sistemas de defesa capazes de interceptar mísseis vindos da Europa ou do Ártico.

A região também é rica em minerais, petróleo e gás natural.

No entanto, a extração mineral enfrenta oposição de povos indígenas e restrições do governo local.

Já a exploração de petróleo e gás é proibida por razões ambientais.

Outro fator que aumenta a importância estratégica da região é o aquecimento do Ártico. O derretimento do gelo tende a ampliar a importância de portos e pode abrir novas rotas de navegação , mudando a dinâmica do comércio internacional.

A China também tem interesse no Ártico. Uma nova rota marítima pela região poderia reduzir a distância percorrida por navios chineses em comparação com rotas tradicionais, além de passar ao lado da Rússia, uma das principais parceiras de Pequim.

Embora esteja distante cerca de 2 mil quilômetros do Ártico, a China investe na construção de navios quebra-gelo. O país também é o maior produtor mundial de carros elétricos e turbinas eólicas, setores que dependem de minerais considerados estratégicos.

A região é ainda importante do ponto de vista militar. Durante a Guerra Fria, russos e americanos mantiveram armas nucleares e submarinos no Ártico. Atualmente, além da disputa militar, a área envolve plataformas de petróleo e gás e rotas de telecomunicações por fibra óptica.

O presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, em entrevista no Salão Oval da Casa Branca, em 2 de setembro de 2026. — Foto: Evelyn Hockstein/ Reuters

O anúncio desta sexta-feira ocorre após meses de tensão e negociações sobre o futuro da segurança da Groenlândia . Trump insistiu diversas vezes que os Estados Unidos deveriam controlar o território e chegou a afirmar que poderia usar a força para isso.

O presidente também ameaçou a União Europeia com tarifas caso a Dinamarca se recusasse a ceder a Groenlândia. As pressões provocaram atritos entre os Estados Unidos e o bloco.

No início deste ano, durante o Fórum Econômico Mundial, em Davos, Trump chamou a Dinamarca de "ingrata" e afirmou que "a Europa não está indo na direção correta". Ele também se referiu à Groenlândia como "um pedaço de gelo" .

Ao fim do encontro, o presidente afirmou que os EUA e a Otan haviam desenhado a estrutura de um possível acordo envolvendo a Groenlândia e toda a região do Ártico.

O presidente também afirmou que há discussões adicionais em andamento sobre o chamado "Domo de Ouro" em relação à Groenlândia, sem fornecer mais informações sobre o projeto.

👉 O Domo de Ouro é uma estrutura militar planejada pelos EUA para interceptar mísseis lançados contra o território norte-americano.

articles.title: Fight intensifies over the fate of homes falling into the sea
articles.summary: California homeowners are building a costly rock wall to hold back the ocean, escalating a battle over private property and what to do about years-long beach...
articles.body:
DANA POINT, California – Natalie Driessen drove down Beach Road on a mission, past neighbors whose houses fell into the sea and others now scrambling to prevent their property from collapsing next.

She had a video from March that she wanted everyone to see. When she spotted an Orange County supervisor outside what was left of one mangled kitchen and living room, Driessen pulled out her phone to play the clip of the California Coastal Commission — the powerful state agency tasked with preserving beaches — discussing a home in her gated community.

California beaches are considered public beyond a certain high tide line, the commissioners warned, and that waterline was rising. "I wonder," one of the commissioners said , "how many years before I'm allowed to just pull up a chair — sit in their, you know, front deck porch and watch TV because it's public land. … I don't think we're that far away from this, right?"

The day's top stories, curated by Washington Post editors. Sign up for free

Storms and high tides — fueled by a near record-breaking El Niño — have battered the California coast in recent weeks, destroying homes and eroding beaches. The fallout has supercharged years-long tensions between the owners of coveted oceanfront property and the authorities they say aren't doing enough to protect them.

The damage has intensified a bigger debate playing out around the coast: What can or should be done to save private property in the most vulnerable communities?

Driessen was furious about the March clip — convinced the authorities wanted her and other beachfront homeowners to give up and leave in the face of sea damage.

"We're paying taxes!" the 51-year-old plastic surgeon told the county supervisor indignantly.

On Beach Road in Dana Point — which has been home and second-home to actors, famous athletes and members of the Disney family — the destruction has residents fuming and banding together. They're organizing in a group chat and paying more than $50,000 per household, they say, to build a rock wall along the shore, desperate and rushing to stave off further damage with another El Niño-driven surge expected in a couple weeks.

Residents want to make the rock wall permanent, but "coastal armoring" is so controversial that the California Coastal Commission generally bans it in new developments.

"It's important to note that while seawalls can provide temporary relief for homes, they can also increase erosion and destroy the public beaches that help protect those same structures," Joshua Smith, a spokesperson for the Coastal Commission, said in a statement.

Smith said the commission has "for years repeatedly engaged the community and the city on medium- to longer-term strategies for preventing flood damage in this area," adding that the agency has suggested installing a cobblestone berm, elevating homes or adding sand to beaches.

The commission approved emergency permits for the Beach Road rock barrier, which it says will cover 17 properties. But many residents are refusing to sign the papers — outraged that they may have to tear the wall down after 120 days if they do not get permanent approval.

Everyone agrees the community, and others like it, need a long-term plan to deal with the eroding beach. But they disagree over what that should look like, and who is to blame for the erupting crisis.

"When we have these emergencies like what happened last week, the responses are ad hoc ... and generally they may not lead to better, good long term outcomes," said Charles Lester, a former Coastal Commission director who now directs an ocean policy center at UC Santa Barbara. "Once the rock goes on the beach it's very hard to bring it back up."

One long-term option for vulnerable communities, Lester said, may be retreat.

"At what point do we start to recognize that maybe it's not a good idea to have the development there?" Lester said. "If we get to that point, the question is not, 'Okay, leave,' it's more like — 'Okay, how do we facilitate a community transition?'"

Replacing the beach sand is another possible solution — but those efforts are expensive and could take years.

"If California is good at anything in this world, it's bureaucracy," Dana Point Mayor John Gabbard lamented in an interview.

The residents of Beach Road know that not everyone sympathizes with wealthy families losing their second homes with ocean views. Driessen sees comments on social media that suggest they deserve the misfortune. Some say they should have seen it coming in the risky business of beachfront real estate.

Driessen says she worked hard for her dream beach house, purchased two years ago. She took out loans and put herself through school.

Now her backyard is destroyed; her home is still standing but at risk whenever the next storm hits.

Driessen's problems started last year, she said, with a sinkhole. By this summer, the holes had multiplied and she called local officials in a panic, saying she worried she would lose the house.

She estimates that she and a neighbor collectively spent more than $400,000 trying to avert disaster, reinforcing a seawall and putting up sandbags.

They raised alarms, she said, but got little help.

She said she tried to rally people into collective action at a neighborhood party in August. "Guys, are we going to wait for someone to get red-tagged?" she remembers asking, using the term for a home marked uninhabitable.

It didn't go anywhere, she said. Then Hurricane Marie hit Southern California this month.

The storm reshaped iconic spots along the coast. In Laguna Beach, officials declared an emergency. In Malibu, dozens of homes were evacuated after a giant sinkhole opened up outside the home of actor Nicolas Cage. In Santa Monica, beach erosion was so bad that officials canceled a music festival scheduled for the end of September.

The storm hit especially hard in Dana Point, a little more than an hour south of Los Angeles.

Away in Hawaii for a wedding, doctor Shalesh Gupta checked video footage from his Beach Road home and realized that his patio collapsed into the ocean. The waves had destroyed his seawall. The bedroom and living room fell next.

Like other homeowners in the area, he said, he only has $250,000 in flood insurance — not enough to cover the loss. His lot is empty. His daughter has urged him to give up on his second home there. "I'm telling you — water is rising, you need to sell the property," he recalled her saying.

Experts say that California could see its highest sea levels ever this winter because of El Niño.

But Gupta and other residents are adamant: They can rebuild with the right protections.

"This problem that we now have was preventable," argued Katrina Foley, the Orange County supervisor who visited Beach Road.

Experts recommended depositing sand decades ago to counter erosion, she said, but local officials didn't do it. Now they are trying to "make up for 50 years of inaction," she said.

The county is working to replenish sand in a few key areas, and officials say those efforts could help other shores such as Beach Road's. Orange County and the city of Dana Point have both declared emergencies, and local officials say they are working with state and federal representatives to get resources.

For now, the Beach Road homeowners are banking on their own temporary solution: the rock wall.

"All of the effort that's happening right now is 100 percent the residents ... everything from manpower to dollars and cents," said Chris Rogers, whose home was largely wrecked.

Driessen and neighbor Steve Watts, 68, stopped outside Gupta's empty lot to chat with one of the men they hired to build their wall. Driessen brought up the video of the Coastal Commission meeting again as waves crashed over their barrier-in-progress.

In her kitchen later, she vented to Watts and another neighbor. "My house was built in 1956, before the Coastal Commission even became a thing," she said. "So I can protect my home."

"Constitutionally, we can all protect our home," Watts said.

Plenty of people disagree with their push to fortify the beach, however.

"The real threat to California's beaches isn't the waves — it's the concrete we pour after they hit," argues a recent op-ed in the San Francisco Chronicle co-written by Lester, the former Coastal Commission director.

California requires local governments to create adaptation plans for sea level rise by 2034. The Coastal Commission has been giving grants for long-term planning , said Kelsey Ducklow, the commission's statewide coastal resilience coordinator.

"What we hope to avoid for all communities is the sort of reactive responses that we're having to see now," Ducklow said.

Watch: Earl Spencer says he's 'telling the truth' about what Charles said after Diana died

Princess Diana's brother has told the BBC exclusively that he is "telling the truth" about a phone call with King Charles in the days after his sister's death.

Earl Spencer claims in a new book the then-Prince of Wales said "we'll forget her soon enough" during an argument over whether Princes William and Harry should walk in Diana's funeral procession.

In a strongly worded response, Buckingham Palace said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".

But in his first interview since, Earl Spencer said: "I can tell you here and now, those are exactly the words he said."

Reacting to the rare statement from the Palace, Earl Spencer said: "Well, is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?."

Speaking to the BBC at his Althorp estate, he added: "I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage of my life.

"I was hyper alert to what he was saying and those are precisely the words that he said and I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. I don't hear him saying he didn't say that."

Pressed on whether he had evidence to back up the claim, he said he told family and friends at the time what had been said "because it was so monstrous".

In response to the Palace disputing his account, Earl Spencer, who shares his first name with the King, said: "They've sort of smudged that one, haven't they? They've said that recollections may vary."

When asked which Charles the public was meant to believe, he said: "I'm telling the truth."

Buckingham Palace declined to give a response to Earl Spencer's fresh comments.

The remarks may bring a renewed focus to the war of words between the Palace and the King's former brother-in-law.

In excerpts of his book published by the Daily Mail, Earl Spencer claims the phone call took place after he insisted Diana would not have wanted the young princes to walk in the procession.

In his BBC interview, he says the King "went ballistic" and "ranted for a while", accusing his family of not having an adequate sense of duty.

"And then he stopped and I thought, oh now, now he's gonna pull himself together and say something more appropriate," Earl Spencer said. "And then, he said, 'we'll forget her soon enough'."

He said he couldn't say exactly what went through his mind at that moment as he was "just so stunned", adding: "I just, after a stunned silence, I said, I cannot believe you just said that. And I hung up on him."

Earl Spencer's book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, is due to be published next week and is expected to be highly critical of the Royal Family.

In further extracts published on Thursday, he claimed how the King "sounded giddily elated" when he called him after Diana's death in a car crash in Paris on 31 August 1997, alleging Charles sounded like a "lottery winner".

Earl Spencer recounts being alerted to the crash by a phone call from his sister Jane in the middle of the night at his home in Cape Town, South Africa.

A call from Charles was among those that followed, and he alleges: "Unlike my other callers, who were stunned, barely able to articulate their condolences and offers of help, he sounded giddily elated - like a lottery winner, I remember thinking at the time."

The death of Diana, a hugely popular figure, created a volatile atmosphere in the country at the time, with the royals accused of failing to show feeling and empathy, and seeming to be out of touch with the public mood.

Earl Spencer's emotional and defiant speech at her funeral added to that cloud of grievance hanging over Diana's death at the age of 36.

Prince Harry has previously said that walking behind his mother's coffin aged 12 was something no child "should be asked to do".

In 2017, he told the BBC he didn't "have an opinion whether that was right or wrong", but "looking back on it", he was glad to have been part of the day.

The full interview with Laura Kuenssberg will be broadcast on BBC One at 18:30 BST on Sunday and be available the same day on BBC iPlayer from 16:00 BST.

articles.title: Trump says the Kennedy Center could be 'ripped down' if he doesn't get 'recognition.' How we got here.
articles.summary: The iconic performing arts venue has been closed since Tuesday. A protest is planned for Friday night.
articles.body:
President Trump was photographed this week on board Air Force One examining a large poster with the words "Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED" printed above a rendering of a construction site, heightening concerns that his administration wants to raze Washington, D.C.'s iconic performing arts venue if his name is not added to its facade.

"I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition," the president told reporters before he boarded the plane Wednesday in North Carolina. "Because frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close. It'll end up being ripped down."

Trump's comments and the photographs that followed are the latest developments in a convoluted saga that started when he dismissed the center's trustees in February 2025 — just days after returning to office — and replaced them with loyalists who elected him chairman.

Despite several legal setbacks, Trump's handpicked board has been pushing ever since to rename the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, which was built as a "living memorial" to the slain 35th president, after the White House's current occupant.

The day before Trump was photographed with the "Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED" poster, his appointees voted to close the center's main building for renovations. Does this mean Trump will bulldoze the Kennedy Center if he doesn't get the "recognition" he wants? Here's what we know — and what we don't.

The Kennedy Center is currently closed. Shortly after 4:30 p.m. on Tuesday, employees heard a sudden notice on the P.A. system: "The center is now closed to the public. Please exit the center by way of the Hall of States." In a statement, officials described the closure as a temporary, emergency action designed to protect people from deteriorating conditions inside the building after a five-foot-long section of ceiling plaster fell during a recent storm.

At the same time, the board has also been locked in a months-long court battle over its renaming and renovation efforts. Just hours before the closure, Federal Judge Casey Cooper again blocked the center from inscribing Trump's name on its facade — and the president himself responded on social media , saying that "the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place" unless an appeals court allows his name back on the building.

"The closing will take place immediately, however, the Renovation and Reconstruction, which is a very large and complex job, cannot begin until such time as the D.C. Circuit rules on the Board's approved name," Trump wrote. "If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is not overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court, the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place."

Last year, Trump demolished the East Wing of the White House after pledging that construction of his new $300 million, 90,000-square-foot ballroom wouldn't "interfere with the current building."

On Thursday, Cooper instructed the center to provide more than 30 days' notice before carrying out any significant changes to its renovation plan, "including but not limited to any 'demolition' of the center's main building."

On Friday, Kerry Kennedy — niece of President Kennedy and daughter of former U.S. Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy — posted on social media that a "Hands Around the Kennedy Center" protest would be taking place at 6:30 p.m. ET.

"With the future still very much uncertain, now more than ever, the Center needs you to stand up for freedom of expression and against authoritarian overreach into arts and culture institutions," read the event's invitation .

On Feb. 7, 2025, Trump announced on social media that he was taking over the Kennedy Center. "At my direction, we are going to make the Kennedy Center in Washington D.C., GREAT AGAIN," he wrote. "I have decided to immediately terminate multiple individuals from the Board of Trustees, including the Chairman, who do not share our Vision for a Golden Age in Arts and Culture."

"We will soon announce a new Board, with an amazing Chairman, DONALD J. TRUMP!" he added.

Within days, Trump had installed his former acting Director of National Intelligence Richard Grenell as interim executive director and replaced the bipartisan board with various allies, including Dana Blumberg (wife of billionaire Robert Kraft), Alison Lutnick (wife of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick), conservative country singer Lee Greenwood, White House deputy chief of staff Dan Scavino, White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and second lady Usha Vance.

At the time, Trump said he objected to previous Kennedy Center programming, citing "Drag Shows specifically targeting our youth." He vowed to oversee the performance schedule himself.

"This marks the first time a president has removed his predecessor's board members at the Kennedy Center and installed himself as chair," the Washington Post reported .

Previously, "political persuasion was never a factor we considered or discussed in artistic programming," Michael Kaiser, the Kennedy Center's president from 2001 to 2014, told the New York Times . "Our Board included 14 members of Congress who were evenly split between the two parties. This balance made it clear to everyone at the center that the only way for us to work was to ignore politics."

In response to Trump's takeover, musician Ben Folds and opera singer Renée Fleming stepped down as the center's artistic advisers; TV producer Shonda Rhimes — formerly treasurer of its board of trustees — left as well. Producers of the musical Hamilton and the play Eureka Day canceled entire planned performance runs. Other artists followed suit.

"These events have caused a major negative reaction in my musical community to playing at the Kennedy Center," guitarist and composer Yasmin Williams wrote in an email to Grenell.

"I cut the DEI bullshit because we can't afford to pay people for fringe and niche programming that the public won't support," Grenell wrote back. Elsewhere, Grenell said that the center had " spent way too much on programming that doesn't bring in any revenue ."

"We have completely reversed the decline of this cherished national institution," Trump claimed in August 2025 . "We ended the woke political programming, and we're restoring the Kennedy Center as the premier venue for performing arts anywhere in the country, anywhere in the world."

Yet a Washington Post analysis conducted in October 2025 found that, after Trump's takeover, ticket sales for orchestra, theater and dance performances at the center plummeted to their lowest level since the COVID-19 pandemic .

In May 2025, the new Kennedy Center board revised its bylaws to exclude the 23 federal and local officials who automatically serve as ex officio members from voting. Going forward, only trustees appointed by Trump would be allowed to vote.

On Dec. 18, 2025 — shortly after Trump became the first president to host the annual Kennedy Center Honors — his appointees voted to rename the venue as The Donald J. Trump and The John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts, or the Trump-Kennedy Center. Then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said the vote was unanimous, but Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty of Ohio, an ex officio board member, insisted that she "was muted on the call and not allowed to speak or voice [her] opposition to this move."

The same day, a new logo featuring Trump's name appeared on the center's website; within 24 hours, workers had added Trump's name to the building's facade. "I was surprised by it, I was honored by it," the president told reporters when asked about the name change. "We saved the building."

Justice Department lawyers later said the new signage had already been " prepared and/or purchased prior to the Board's vote the day before ."

In protest, more artists canceled planned performances, including Kristy Lee, Chuck Redd and Philip Glass. The Washington National Opera announced it would leave the center.

"The Kennedy Center is a living memorial to a fallen president and named for President Kennedy by federal law," former Massachusetts Rep. Joe Kennedy III, RFK's grandson, wrote on social media. "It can no sooner be renamed than can someone rename the Lincoln Memorial, no matter what anyone says.

In late December, Beatty filed suit against the Kennedy Center trustees who voted to change the name, arguing that they had no legal power to do so.

A few months later, in May 2026, Cooper sided with Beatty and ordered the center to revert to its original name within 14 days. The center's founding statute "makes crystal clear that the Center is to be named for President Kennedy, and it cannot bear any other formal name or public memorial based on the Board's unilateral say-so," Cooper wrote in his opinion . "Congress gave the Kennedy Center its name, and only Congress can change it."

By mid-June, Trump's name had been removed from the center's website and facade. But the board also tried to appeal Cooper's ruling, arguing that millions of dollars in donations would have to be returned if the center did not ultimately bear Trump's name, according to its new bylaws.

These efforts failed, yet Trump's appointees seem undeterred. Last month, they voted to inscribe "Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump" below the center's name on the building's facade — which led Cooper to again block the board from adding the president's name to the building.

"Simply put, defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress's blessing," Cooper wrote. "The board resolution bucks a federal court order and a statute Congress enacted."

Renovation or demolition… or something else?

In tandem with its renaming efforts, the board has also spent the last seven months pushing to shutter the center for renovations.

Trump started to muse about the project in late 2025. The following February, he announced the center would close on July 4, 2026, for a two-year renovation. "I have determined that The Trump Kennedy Center, if temporarily closed for Construction, Revitalization, and Complete Rebuilding, can be, without question, the finest Performing Arts Facility of its kind, anywhere in the World," he wrote on social media.

But in his May ruling, Cooper also issued a temporary order blocking the center from fully closing for two years. Instead, he said the center could "move ahead with renovations to the decades-old building and could later decide to close … after its board more fully considered the impact on its statutory requirement to maintain some programming at all times," according to CNN .

At the time, skeptics questioned whether major renovations were necessary, noting that Trump had previously said the center would remain " fully open during construction, renovation and beautification ."

"Trump's contradictory statements and the absence of an independent board or any notification to Congress make these claims of a building in need of repair unverifiable at best," the Atlantic wrote . "A more plausible reason for the closing is that under Trump, the Kennedy Center can't hold on to staff, artists or audiences."

According to a Washington Post analysis published in August and based on confidential internal documents, "ticket sales had already dropped in the 10 months following Trump's takeover" — "but both ticket sales and donations plunged after the Trump-led board of trustees voted in December to rename the center after him and put his name on the front of the building." As of June, the center's own officials were projecting a $100 million revenue shortfall for fiscal year 2026, with a 70% decline in earned income, the Post reported.

In response, Trump and his administration have argued that they inherited a "decrepit" structure in dire need of repairs — repairs that cannot proceed unless the president gets credit for them.

"An order blocking the Board from appropriately recognizing President Trump will cause donors to flee, financial contributions to dry up and structural rehabilitation to stop," the Department of Justice wrote in an Aug. 29 filing , adding that without Trump's efforts, "the Center will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down" — possibly to be replaced with "a large outdoor amphitheater overlooking the Potomac River."

Such a venue has "been proposed, by some, for many years," the filing said.

articles.title: TfW pay-as-you-go risks overcharging train passengers, says Flintshire council
articles.summary: Flintshire council said Transport for Wales' new system charges all users an adult fare.
articles.body:
A council has warned that Transport for Wales' (TfW) pay-as-you-go system could leave some rail passengers paying more - as it charges all users an adult fare.

TfW recently launched a social media campaign to promote the payment system's availability to passengers on the 27-mile (44 km) Wrexham-Bidston Borderlands Line.

A TikTok advert for the scheme tells viewers it offers passengers TfW's "best value fare".

But Flintshire council said there had been no explanation that children, families and pensioners, who all qualified for concessionary fares, would be charged full adult price.

TfW said it was "actively reviewing" how to communicate alternative ticketing options to customers.

The pay-as-you-go scheme allows customers to use a tap-in and tap-out process using a contactless debit card or smartphone device without needing to buy tickets in advance for adult single journeys.

Alasdair Ibbotson, a councillor for Penyffordd, first raised the concern that passengers were being overcharged by the system in July.

He told a council meeting that signage around stations did not explain that concessionary travel would not be supported.

Ibbotson criticised the messaging that pay-as-you-go offers the "best value fares" as it was possible for some passengers to pay less through concessionary travel.

"The tap‑and‑go machines can only charge full‑fare adult tickets," he said.

"If you are eligible to travel on a child ticket or at a reduced rate because you have a railcard you will not be charged the correct fare for your journey.

"You will be overcharged. So the notion that this is the best value fare is categorically untrue."

He told the meeting there had been small print on station banners that stated the value claim was compared to equivalent TfW tickets – but the system only measured against a full adult fare.

However, he claimed the social adverts gave no indication that tap-and-go fares were not the cheapest for everyone.

The council has now warned rail passengers to check whether a cheaper travel option is available to them before using pay-as-you-go.

Glyn Banks, cabinet member for waste and transportation, said it was a "convenient option", but it was "important" that passengers understood it was not always the cheapest choice.

He said people could save money by buying tickets in advance, using travel passes or railcards, and that pay-as-you-go did not support railcard discounts, child, family or return tickets.

"We've asked TfW to make it clearer for passengers when travelling as tap and go calculates the standard adult single fare for your tapped journey," he said.

"We hope this issue can be addressed as soon as possible to ensure passengers are not disadvantaged."

The council's chief executive Neil Cockerton had also written to TfW asking for new signage to be installed at stations, in order to inform passengers that they may be able to access cheaper tickets through other payment methods.

TfW said it was committed to making rail travel "as simple, convenient, and affordable as possible" for customers.

A spokesperson said: "While railcard and concessionary discounts are not yet supported via pay as you go, advice on alternative ticketing options is available on our website, at stations and through customer channels.

"We are actively reviewing how we communicate this to customers."

TfW said it was exploring a pilot to allow eligible railcards to be linked to pay-as-you-go accounts, and hoped to introduce child fares in future, but said further development was needed.

The spokesperson said: "Free concessionary travel and family or group offers are not in scope for our pay-as-you-go offering. The latter position is aligned with that of most other pay as you go schemes nationwide.

"We remain focused on making rail travel easier, more flexible, and better value."

The rail company said further details on improvements to its pay-as-you-go scheme would be announced in due course.

articles.title: 'Not an easy inbox' for new Scottish Labour leader
articles.summary: Anas Sarwar's replacement will be named later and has big challenges set out already.
articles.body:
There's an old joke involving someone asking for directions, and the reply comes: "Well, if I were you, I wouldn't start from here."

And that's probably the (unhelpful) advice a lot of people would give the next Scottish Labour leader.

It's a job that will go to one of two MSPs this weekend - Michael Marra or Joe Fagan.

The victor will inherit a party that had a historically bad result in May's Scottish Parliament election. They will lead a group of just 17 MSPs.

That makes them the joint second largest party at Holyrood, tied with Reform UK, but there remains a gulf between Labour and their SNP rivals.

Anas Sarwar fell well short of his goal to become First Minister of Scotland, and swapped Holyrood for the House of Lords shortly afterwards.

It has been revealed during the contest to find Sarwar's successor that the party's membership has slumped to around 11,000.

You can see why it's a less-than-ideal starting point.

So what are the challenges facing the next leader? And what – if anything – can they do to get the Scottish Labour show back on the road?

We asked the pollster Mark Diffley to spell out some of the issues that Marra or Fagan will have to tackle.

He didn't mince his words: "The party has become a bit of an irrelevance, and I think that is the biggest hurdle that they face going forward.

"The vast majority of people don't really know either of the candidates and, worryingly for them, don't know that the contest is going on".

So what does the pollster think the winner needs to do?

Diffley spells out three priorities: become relevant, develop a relationship with the prime minister (who he says is currently popular in Scotland) and spell out appealing policies.

Some aspects of that will be easier than others.

One senior party insider agreed with much of Mark Diffley's analysis, warning "it's not an easy inbox".

They told me there's a need to change approach, and Labour might look to learn from a rival party – the Scottish Greens.

The Green strategy has been to get their policies taken on by the SNP. You'll often hear the Greens talk about Scottish government decisions and essentially say: 'that was our idea'.

And Labour, this insider argues, should be taking the same approach.

There could be offers to back SNP budgets in return for more public control of buses or higher wages for care workers, for example.

At future elections, Labour could then have tangible "wins" to point at.

It would be a change in approach from a party that tended to oppose or abstain on budgets in the last parliament.

It's a view shared by another party figure, who called for a constant "SNP bad" approach to be ditched, saying "the electorate rejected that wholesale".

They added that Scottish Labour had to be "far more considerate about where we pick our battles", and said that they should approach SNP policies, like cutting the number of health boards, constructively.

And that's not the only pressing issue the new leader may have to address.

While many think Andy Burnham has had a good start as prime minister, there is concern within Scottish Labour about some aspects of Number 10's approach north of the border.

Some told me they believe the prime minister should have made more visits to Scotland. And another said Downing Street had been "a bit all over the shop" when it came to a second independence referendum.

And that brings us to an age old area that could prove tricky for the next leader: the constitution.

Andy Burnham seemed to set hares running last week in the Commons when he suggested there was a scenario where a second Scottish independence referendum could be on the table.

His spokesperson quickly rowed back on the comments, but SNP figures couldn't believe their luck when the door seemed to be opened (even just slightly) to a second vote.

It's an issue that the new leader of Scottish Labour will have to engage with.

Both candidates have, at times in this contest, seemed to struggle to articulate exactly where Scottish Labour stands on the question of a second referendum.

Perhaps one area where the new leader may have a slightly easier time is managing their group of MSPs.

It would be a bit of a mean joke to say this is easy when there's not that many of them - but there's an element of truth here for Scottish Labour.

This hasn't been a particularly ill-tempered contest, and there aren't vast ideological differences between Joe Fagan and Michael Marra.

The loser in the contest is unlikely to make life particularly difficult for the winner.

Although it's important to note that this contest hasn't been a bed of roses, with Monica Lennon labelling the party "quite nasty" when she failed to make the final leadership ballot.

But the overall state of Scottish Labour, and its pattern of decline at Holyrood, will be the most pressing concern for the winner.

The party is in a hole, and getting out of it will fall to either Joe Fagan or Michael Marra.

Getting this movement to a more positive destination is possible, but it looks like a gruelling task.

Perhaps they wouldn't want to start from here, but they don't get a say in that.

articles.title: Daisy Edgar-Jones: I'm like my character in Sense and Sensibility
articles.summary: In real life the actress says she is just like the character she's playing in Sense and Sensibility.
articles.body:
Daisy Edgar-Jones has been well cast in her new film.

She plays Elinor, the rational elder sister in Sense and Sensibility, opposite the younger, more romantic sister Marianne.

Speaking to the BBC, Edgar-Jones says that in her personal life, she really is like her character.

"When it comes to love, I think I am very much more Elinor in every sort of way," she says.

"I definitely lead a lot with my head and try and push aside, bury my emotion."

But she notes that one of the joys of the film is seeing Elinor learn to enjoy a "wilder, passionate side" of herself. "And I feel like I learnt to do that too," she says.

Best known for starring in hit TV series Normal People with Paul Mescal, Edgar-Jones, 28, is now taking on a lead role in the latest adaptation of Jane Austen's book.

Ahead of its release, she’s been talking to me about whether we really need another Sense and Sensibility film (spoiler: yes. “The more the merrier, in my opinion.”)

She also told me why young people today can still see themselves in Jane Austen's stories - and gave me her take on whether her friend and former co-star Mescal should be the next James Bond .

The new film, directed by Georgia Oakley, follows the Dashwood sisters as they navigate their way through love, loss and societal expectations, following the death of their father.

It's a classic adaptation of Austen's novel, rather than a more contemporary take.

When I meet Edgar-Jones at a hotel in central London, I ask her whether there was ever a temptation to make it more "2026".

"It does feel very much like it's honouring the period," she agrees, "but I think there's a freshness to the filmmaking that I think is really beautiful".

She is starring alongside Esmé Creed-Miles, 26, who plays her sister Marianne.

Together, the two sisters' different approaches to life are characterised as "sense" (Elinor) and "sensibility" (Marianne).

Creed-Miles is also well cast, it seems. "I'm more like Marianne [than Elinor], yeah, which is annoying sometimes," she laughs.

Sense and Sensibility has been adapted for screen countless times before - including the hit 1995 film starring Emma Thompson and Kate Winslet.

Edgar-Jones loves that version (“one of my favourite films of all time”) but also feels there's room to tell Austen’s classic tale again.

"Her stories are something that fascinate us still today,” she says.

It was also easy for her and Creed-Mills to build the sisterly rapport on screen, as they previously worked together as teenagers on the 2018 film Pond Life.

“We had a real laugh," Creed-Mills says of their time on that film. "We would have sleepovers every night and watch Love Island."

For Edgar-Jones, the theme of sisterhood is something that stuck with her from Sense and Sensibility - despite her being an only child in real life.

“I've heard a lot of people say that after watching the film, it either makes them want a sister or to ring up their sister and say like, ‘Hey, I love you,’ and I think that's really special. It's the part of the film I'm most proud of.”

Jane Austen seems to be everywhere right now.

Last year marked the 250th anniversary of her birth and, in recent years, we've enjoyed two BBC TV series, Miss Austen and The Other Bennet Sister, the West End's Clueless musical (based on the cult 90s teen film adaptation of Emma), and Ava Pickett's modern stage adaptation of Emma .

There's also a new adaptation of Pride and Prejudice written by Dolly Alderton and starring Emma Corrin coming to Netflix.

For Edgar-Jones, the themes in Austen's books are just as revelant today.

"She has an incredible way of articulating the female experience," she says.

"Her ruminations on love, on romance, on sisterly love, on family dynamics, on interpersonal social dynamics - she's such a talent."

Austen also wrote about the sort of dating behaviour that people complain about on TikTok (like situationships and ghosting), before terms like that had even been invented. Does that help Gen Z audiences relate to her, I ask?

"We still have the same human heart as we did 200 years ago. Our capacity to love and feel heartbreak, and that early first love feeling, is something that we all experience in various ways.

"And so yes, I think definitely the trials and tribulations of the two women [Elinor and Marianne] as they navigate life, love and all that becomes as you grow up, definitely is so relatable to all generations."

"These women are very relatable," agrees Creed-Mills.

"I don't know if seeing a movie is going to fix everything, but it might make you feel a little bit less alone in some of the things you're feeling."

Edgar-Jones shot to fame during the pandemic with her role in Normal People.

Based on Sally Rooney's novel, the BBC Three drama charted the on-off relationship of teenagers Marianne and Connell, played by Edgar-Jones and Paul Mescal.

The pair have remained close (a few years ago, Edgar-Jones told me Mescal was "one of my all-time best friends") - and both are now successful actors.

Edgar-Jones has since starred in Twisters and Where The Crawdads Sing, while Mescal was in Gladiator II, Hamnet and will be in the Beatles films.

So, is he really in the running? Edgar-Jones didn’t give too much away.

“I don’t know, but I think there’s nothing Paul can’t do,” she says.

“So I would be there. Wow, that’s cool.”

Sense and Sensibility is out in UK cinemas on 25 September.

articles.title: UK weather: Summer warmth to return next week with 26C forecast
articles.summary: After a changeable week, drier and warmer conditions will dominate for some next week, but with little rain for those who need it.
articles.body:
Temperatures could peak at 26C next week as late summer warmth returns to parts of the UK.

Southern areas will experience the highest temperatures, but most locations will be warmer than normal for late September.

Warmth could last all week for some in England and Wales, but it might only be a short-lived boost for Scotland and Northern Ireland.

The high pressure, which is responsible for the warmth, will also mean little rain for places continuing to experience drought conditions.

The changeable conditions that have dominated the past week will continue into the weekend, with blustery winds coming in off the Atlantic and gales for some western coasts and hills.

While Saturday will become a day of sunshine and passing showers for many, in southern parts of England and Wales a weather front draped across the area will mean mostly cloudy conditions and rain or drizzle at times, especially in the south-west.

Despite the cloud, it will feel warm and humid due to the south-westerly winds dragging in warm and moist air from the mid-Atlantic.

The much more autumnal look to the weather charts at the moment is down to a particularly brisk and straight jet stream roaring through the skies across the Atlantic.

It has meant rain-bearing areas of lower pressure to the north of the UK, high pressure to the south and stronger winds in between, creating the changeable conditions.

However, as the jet stream starts to buckle through the second half of the weekend the weather will slowly being to calm down.

On Sunday, early rain in the far north and south of the UK should move away to leave most parts dry with sunny spells by the afternoon.

Strong winds in north-east Scotland should ease too. While it will feel pleasant in the sunshine, temperatures will be close to the seasonal average of 15-21 Celsius.

Warmth returns next week with break from rain

Into the start of next week, high pressure will build across the UK more widely at first.

Other than early rain in Scotland and northern England, most places will see increasing amounts of sunshine breaking through during the day.

Temperatures will lift by a degree or so compared to Sunday and humidity levels will creep up too.

That more humid air paired with light winds across England and Wales into Tuesday means some will start off rather misty and foggy.

Once the sun has broken through though, it will feel like late summer warmth has returned.

Temperatures could peak at around 25 or 26 Celsius in south-east England, but reach the low 20s in many other parts of England, Wales, Northern Ireland and Eastern Scotland.

2026 has already been a record-breaking year for the number of days above 25C, with last week exceeding the record of 89 days set in 1959.

A weather front moving into western Scotland is likely to bring some rain and could be the focus for a developing low pressure system that will bring more widespread rain midweek across the northern half of the UK.

As high pressure holds on across the south, many will stay largely dry and warm here through the rest of the week.

While many may enjoy the warm weather, it is not good news for declining reservoir and water storage levels.

While recent rain has been welcome, it has been well short of what is required to break the drought across most of England and Wales.

By Friday morning Leconfield, East Yorkshire had only received 11% of its normal September rainfall, and Durham just 14% - both well below the 50-60% that would be typical by now.

Some forecasts do show the potential for rain returning more widely from late week and into next, but others hint at continuing high pressure and potentially even warmer air.

articles.title: Ekurhuleni killings: Grim discoveries of murdered women spark fear in South Africa
articles.summary: Dineo Motapane is one of nine recent victims whose deaths have left a nation traumatised over the level of violence against women.
articles.body:
"What we are going to do, I have no idea," sobs Nokwanda Matshikiza, reflecting on the murder of her niece Dineo Motapane. "But something must give."

"For us, for all the other women. How many other bodies will be found before something happens?"

Nokwanda is speaking to the BBC from the family home near South Africa's main city, Johannesburg, just two days after relatives identified Dineo's body.

The 38-year-old mother-of-two was last seen alive last Sunday. Her battered body, partly burned, found later in the residential region of Ekurhuleni.

Nokwanda weeps as she describes how the family will have to face, at some point, the grim task of telling Dineo's daughter of her death.

"How do you explain that your parent was brutally murdered, dumped in a field, and just left there, discarded like a piece of rubbish.

"There's no coming to peace with it," she adds. "It's something that you can never reconcile yourself with, that you can never get over."

Dineo's death this week has come amid a series of comparable incidents in Ekurhuleni – her body one of three discovered there this week. In total, nine bodies of murdered women have been found in similar circumstances in the region since July.

The problem has always been there but this spate of grim discoveries has once again sparked a national outcry about the scale of violence against women in the country – which has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence in the world.

Themba Kekana is also living in shock at the death of a loved one.

His sister, Itumeleng, was one of the first to disappear in Ekurhuleni.

The 32-year-old shopkeeper's body was found in July, 17 days after she was last seen alive. Her body was badly bruised, partially clothed and dumped on a bridge.

"We are devastated with grief," says Themba, wet eyes shining.

"I look at my sister's young daughter and my eyes fill with tears, I know there is no way that I can ever take this pain away from her.

"No family should have to deal with what we are faced with."

Only one arrest has been made in connection with the murders – and that was two days after the first body was discovered on 15 July.

Nobody has been detained following the murders of Itumeleng or Dineo or the other six Ekurhuleni women.

Most of the victims were young, in their 20s or 30s, and almost all had suffered extreme violence before their deaths.

Police have said they are not sure if they are hunting a serial killer. It is possible the cases are not linked.

Either way, what has happened in this residential district east of South Africa's biggest city has traumatised the nation, shining a spotlight on a situation that many believe is a crisis.

South Africa's police issue detailed crime statistics every quarter, which show that during the last quarter – between April and June this year - 5,427 people were murdered.

The official data does not distinguish between the genders of the victims, but this week the country's Human Rights Commission released figures showing that 569 women had been killed in that period (six a day on average), with another 1,052 who faced attempted murder.

Many women - already feeling unsafe - have been left reeling by recent events.

And it has put pressure on the government, less than a year after ministers acknowledged the scale of the issue and declared gender-based violence a national disaster.

Announcing the move last November, Minister of Social Development Nokuzola Sisisi Tolashe said treating the issue as a national disaster would help the government tackle the crisis.

It followed weeks of protests, culminating in a "Women's Shut Down" march as South Africa hosted the G20 summit.

This week has seen a chorus of calls for things to go further.

Rights group Amnesty International said an important first step towards protecting South Africa's women was to recognise femicide as a separate crime.

"Every day that femicide remains unrecognised as a crime is a failure to confront the targeted killing of women," said Amnesty's country director Shenilla Mohamed in a statement. "It is time to call it what it is: Femicide.

"Femicide is a gender-motivated crime. It is the killing of a woman because she is a woman."

Amnesty says femicide is criminalised as a specific crime in 33 countries, including Gabon and Morocco in Africa.

It argues that making that change in South Africa could help focus on the scale of the issue.

"It would compel the state to confront their failure to protect women and girls from violence," says Mohamed. "You cannot fix what you are not tracking."

Almost everyone in South Africa agrees more needs to be done.

President Cyril Ramaphosa this week pledged to leave "no stone unturned" in investigating the crimes in Ekurhuleni, adding: "As a nation, we must stand up for the rights, safety and dignity of women and girls."

Lebogang Ramofoko, an advocate for gender and social justice, said the levels of violence against women in the country were symptomatic of a much bigger problem – a lack of regard for humanity.

"The bodies of black women have been treated as disposable in this country for time in memorial, passed down from colonisation through to apartheid," she tells the BBC, referring to the legalised system of racism that was in place until 1994.

"What we see happening to women is testimony to legacies of violence from those systems whose traumas were never addressed.

"This is not to say black men are inherently violent, but in systems where violence was meted out against them for decades, historically black women were the people that that violence would be taken out on - that cycle has not been broken."

In Kempton Park, a district of Ekurhuleni where five of the nine recent bodies were found, Lumka Maqhubela is part of the Girl2Woman Foundation group which has held protests to raise awareness of the crimes.

"We are grieved, we are scared," she says. "If the police cannot protect us any more the government should step in and do something.

"It's clear that we are not safe, we cannot be told by the police to be more vigilant. They should be doing more to make our communities safe – what else are we expected to do? We are not safe anywhere, not in our homes, not in the streets, it needs to stop."

"I feel uncomfortable," says Thulisile Sibande, 32. "When I go to a shop, I have to look around. I'm shocked and scared. So scared, it's a trauma."

Thembi Mabena, 60, tells the BBC she lived in the same neighbourhood as Dineo Motapane.

"She was laughing every day, with everybody," she remembers. "Now I'm worried.

"I know many children, girls, who tell me they are afraid to go to the shop alone. There is no safety, even for me too. I am old, but there is no safety."

"In South Africa," says Lerato Mzizi, 20, simply, "women are not safe any more."
